research_questions: What is the metaphor of sight and blindness across the full story?
How do linguistic markers of evasion, assumption and conversational turn-taking reveal the underlying information asymmetry and mutual deception between the narrator and the girl?

claims.statement: Imagined sight (memory, guesswork, the mind's eye) is concentrated in the middle of the story, where the narrator performs being sighted.
claims.evidence: only 1 hit(s) of imagined sight were found, too few to judge

claims.statement: The language of pretence and concealment runs through the conversation with the girl, while the language of revelation is concentrated at the end.
claims.evidence: 3 of 3 pretence and concealment hits fall in Stages I–III; no revelation hits were found

claims.statement: Markers of evasion and assumption appear in the girl's speech as well as in the narrator's narration and speech, so the deception is mutual in the language and not only in the plot.
claims.evidence: the girl's speech has 0 markers (0.00 per 100 words); the narrator's narration and speech have 8 (0.88 per 100 words)

claims.statement: Turn-taking is densest while the narrator and the girl are talking, and becomes sparser after she leaves.
claims.evidence: turn-taking has 2.08 hits per 100 words in Stages I–III and 2.14 in Stage IV

dimensions.label: Sight and blindness
dimensions.definition: The language of seeing and not seeing, used literally and as metaphor, and the senses that stand in for sight.

subs.label: Literal sight
subs.definition: Eyes, seeing, looking, noticing, light and darkness, and blindness as physical facts.

items.phrase: I was totally blind at the time
my eyes sensitive only to light and darkness
staring into the daylight that was darkness for me

subs.label: Imagined sight
subs.definition: Seeing in memory, imagination or guesswork: pictures formed without the eyes.

items.phrase: in my mind's eye I could see telegraph posts flashing by
She had beautiful eyes but they were of no use to her. She was completely blind. Didn’t you notice

subs.label: Substitute senses
subs.definition: Hearing, touch and smell used in place of sight: voices, sounds, scents and the feel of things.

items.phrase: I heard you come in
the sound of her slippers
I heard the panting of the engine, the rumble of the wheels
I wanted to raise my hand and touch her hair but she moved away

dimensions.label: Performance and concealment
dimensions.definition: Acts that pretend to see, hide a lack of sight, or expose what was hidden.

subs.label: Pretence
subs.definition: Actions and remarks that act out sight in front of another person (turning to the window, describing a view, commenting on someone's appearance).

items.phrase: I didn’t see you either
She was an interesting girl

subs.label: Concealment
subs.definition: Words that show a character hiding something, fearing discovery or playing a part.

items.phrase: I wondered if I would be able to prevent her from discovering that I was blind
I knew that there were hardly any animals left in the forests near Dehra
I don’t remember

subs.label: Revelation
subs.definition: Words that expose what was hidden, or show that something was not noticed.

items.phrase: She had beautiful eyes but they were of no use to her. She was completely blind

dimensions.label: Evasion and assumption
dimensions.definition: How each speaker avoids giving information and guesses at what the other knows.

subs.label: Evasion
subs.definition: Replies that deflect, generalise, joke or change the subject instead of answering directly.

items.phrase: I ventured, ‘that the trees seem to be moving while we seem to be standing still?’
I thought, then, that I would try to laugh for her, but the thought of laughter only made me feel troubled and lonely
Can you tell me—did she keep her hair long or short

subs.label: Assumption
subs.definition: Guesses, inferences and markers of uncertainty about the other person or the world (probably, perhaps, must have, seemed, I suppose, I wondered).

items.phrase: They have too much to take in, I suppose
Aunts are usually formidable creatures
I wondered if my words had touched her or whether she thought me a romantic fool
Had she noticed already that I could not see
Oh, so you do have a pretty face, thought I
I wondered if she wore her hair in a bun or if it was plaited. Perhaps it was hanging loose over her shoulders. Or was it cut very short

subs.label: Face work
subs.definition: Compliments, polite formulas and gallantry that protect each speaker's self-image and smooth over what is not said.

items.phrase: Then I had better not get too familiar
‘You are a very gallant young man’
You must be disappointed

dimensions.label: Conversational turn-taking
dimensions.definition: How the conversation is organised: who asks, who answers, and where it stops.

subs.label: Questions
subs.definition: Questions asked by any speaker, copied as whole questions.

items.phrase: Are you going all the way to Dehra
Where are you going
‘What is it like outside?’
‘Why don’t you look out of the window?’
‘Have you noticed,’ I ventured, ‘that the trees seem to be moving while we seem to be standing still?’
‘Do you see any animals?’

subs.label: Turn markers
subs.definition: Speech verbs and phrases that open or close a turn or attribute it to a speaker (I asked, she said, I ventured).

items.phrase: I asked
She said
I said
‘That always happens,’ she said
‘You have an interesting face,’ I remarked
‘It’s nice to be told I have an interesting face. I’m tired of people telling me I have a pretty face.’
‘You are a very gallant young man,’ she said
‘But why are you so serious?’
‘We’ll soon be at your station,’ I said
‘She was an interesting girl,’ I said
‘I don’t remember,’ he said sounding puzzled
‘You must be disappointed,’ he said

subs.label: Silence and closure
subs.definition: Silences, pauses, interruptions, farewells and the ending of the conversation.

items.phrase: She was silent
I turned from the window and faced the girl and for a while we sat in silence
There was some confusion in the doorway
Then the door banged and the world was shut out again

figures.title: Figure 1. Where does each dimension appear in the story?
figures.how: Each row is one dimension and each column is one segment of the story, in order. The number in each square is the number of hits; the shade shows hits per 100 words, so short and long segments can be compared. Dotted red lines mark where a new stage begins.
figures.shows: Sight and blindness is densest in segment 6 (At the window: the pretence of looking: 2.2 per 100 words) and absent from segments 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12; performance and concealment is densest in segment 3 (The resolve to hide, and the aunt at Saharanpur: 1.7 per 100 words) and absent from segments 1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12; evasion and assumption is densest in segment 5 ("What is it like outside?": 3.6 per 100 words) and absent from segments 1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11; turn-taking is densest in segment 8 (Gallant and serious, and the journey's end: 5.9 per 100 words) and absent from segments 1, 3, 9, 10.

figures.title: Figure 2. Which sub-types are strongest, and where?
figures.how: Each row is one sub-type (the number in brackets is its dimension). Each bubble is a segment. A bigger bubble means more phrases of that sub-type in that segment.
figures.shows: The largest sub-types are turn markers (13 hits), questions (6 hits), assumption (5 hits). No hits were found for: revelation.

figures.title: Figure 3. How do the stages differ?
figures.how: The story is grouped into four stages. Each bar shows hits per 100 words, so a longer stage does not look stronger only because it is longer.
figures.shows: Sight and blindness peaks in Stage I (1.31 per 100 words; range 0.00 to 1.31); performance and concealment peaks in Stage I (0.65 per 100 words; range 0.00 to 0.65); evasion and assumption peaks in Stage I (0.98 per 100 words; range 0.43 to 0.98); turn-taking peaks in Stage II (3.80 per 100 words; range 0.98 to 3.80).

figures.title: Figure 4. How does each dimension change across the story?
figures.how: Each line is one dimension followed across the segments in story order, in hits per 100 words. A rising line means that the dimension grows denser as the story moves on.
figures.shows: Sight and blindness shows no steady trend (rho = -0.29) and moves in bursts; performance and concealment shows no steady trend (rho = -0.40) and moves in bursts; evasion and assumption shows no steady trend (rho = -0.22) and moves in bursts; turn-taking shows no steady trend (rho = +0.02) and moves in bursts.

figures.title: Figure 5. Which phrases carry the most weight?
figures.how: The fifteen most frequent phrases in the extraction, coloured by dimension.
figures.shows: The most frequent items are "I said" (3), "I asked" (2), "my eyes sensitive only to light and darkness" (1), "I was totally blind at the time" (1), "the sound of her slippers" (1). Together, the 15 most frequent items account for 18 of the 42 hits.

figures.title: Figure 6. Whose words carry each dimension?
figures.how: Each group of bars is one voice: the narrator's narration and thoughts, the narrator speaking aloud, the girl, and the man who boards at Saharanpur. Each bar shows hits per 100 words of that voice, so the girl's short speeches can be compared with the narrator's long narration.
figures.shows: Sight and blindness is densest in the narrator's narration and thoughts (0.96 per 100 words); performance and concealment is densest in the narrator's speech (0.56 per 100 words); evasion and assumption is densest in the narrator's speech (1.67 per 100 words); turn-taking is densest in the narrator's speech (6.11 per 100 words). The girl's 135 words contain 6 hits in all; the man's 55 words contain 2.
